text:
Quick Take:
A slim, freestanding shoe cabinet that holds more than expected—including boots thanks to the adjustable shelf. Easy enough to assemble, but it must be anchored for safety.

Pros:
-Narrow profile works in small entryways and hallways
-Adjustable inner shelf allows storage of larger boots
-Holds about 6 pairs of shoes in the top drawer, or 3 pairs of large shoes plus kids’ shoes in the bottom
-Clear instructions and straightforward assembly (similar to IKEA furniture)
-Keeps shoes hidden and entryway neat
-Good price for the functionality

Cons:
-Small gaps at the bottom of drawers make it look slightly unfinished
-Top drawer rubs a bit at the top when opening
-Laminate finish isn’t very thick
-Lightweight build requires anchoring for stability
-Doesn’t sit flush to wall if you have base moulding (though anchor is adjustable)

Full Review:
I needed something to tame the pile of shoes in my really non-existent entryway/kitchen, and this shoe cabinet has been the perfect solution. The narrow profile doesn’t block the doorway, but it still holds a surprising number of shoes. The adjustable inner shelf is especially helpful—I can fit up to 6 pairs of regular shoes in the top drawer, and the bottom fits about 3 pairs of large shoes plus, I would assume small kids’ shoes, when adjusted for boots.

There are some minor quirks. There’s a small gap at the bottom of both drawers, which helps them open smoothly but looks a little odd. The top of the upper drawer rubs slightly at the top when opening. The laminate finish also isn’t very thick, but overall the piece feels durable enough for everyday use.

Assembly wasn’t too bad if you’re used to IKEA-style furniture. The instructions were clear, and everything came together as expected. The unit is lightweight, so it absolutely needs to be anchored to the wall—otherwise it can tip forward when opening heavy drawers full of shoes. Because of my base moulding, it doesn’t sit completely flush to the wall, but the anchor was adjustable enough to make it work.

Overall, this cabinet keeps my entryway tidy, makes the space feel so much more organized, and is a good price for the amount of storage and function you get. Not perfect, but very practical and a great fit for small spaces.

Fan noise at 2800rpm. Makes a grinding noise at 75% fan speed. AMD drivers have the fan speed set to 100% by default at minimal heat.  I have mine at -35mv and -10 power limit. This card is a compact card at the cost of vram temps. It does run a lot cooler than my 6800XT I can say. Really if you had a fan on the side of the case these newer cards will run much cooler. Or an open case.  There is a 28c delta between the hotspot and gpu temp sensors which isn't good. I believe these early cards need to have thermal paste re-applied to the die. But doing so voids the warranty. I really want to do this with my card. All of the heat is coming from the left side of the card mounted in my pc. Also you need a bigger case for airflow with these 300 watt or higher gpus. I have a 4000D case and it's a glass side panel. You need something with a mesh side panel or vents on the side panel for the airflow of these high wattage cards. I have 5 120mm fans and it's not enough for the heat this card puts out. text:
This is an attractive 5-Tier bookcase. Just some things to be aware of:

NOTE: TO ENSURE A STURDY BUILT THIS BOOKCASE WILL REQUIRE WOOD GLUE ON ALL CONNECTING JOINTS: SEE BELOW.

1) The height of the shelves is not high enough for an 8.5" x 11" periodical. If you're planning on placing standard-size paper or folders into a shelf this will not hold them. Smaller books and periodicals will work.

2) Instructions: I've had lots of experience building such furniture and this is an easy build, but you do have to be careful to screw the pieces together so that the finished ends that you see (the laminated ends and not the raw pressed wood) face the front... this may seem obvious but bears mentioning anyhow. The instructions are minimal with illustrations numbered step 1, step, 2.... etc. It's easy enough to follow.

3) Wood Glue Required: This is very important. The thickness of the pressed wood is around 1/2". The instructions do not mention this, but I will: YOU MUST USE WOOD GLUE ON ALL JOINTS because screws alone will not make this bookcase study and rigid enough using just the supplied screws. I would also add that IF YOU ARE NOT SURE HOW TO USE WOOD GLUE ON JOINTS DO NOT PURCHASE THIS BOOKCASE - OR FIND SOMEONE THAT KNOWS HOW TO WORK WITH WOOD.

4) This is the only tricky part: The bookcase is made up of 2 sections, one taller than the other and then they are screwed together using the supplied screws and 4 special circular clamping bolts. Be careful when inserting the clamping bolts so that they are placed into the proper holes on the shelf section that joins both sections. Pay careful attention to the diagram that shows the screws and the special clamping bolts and be sure you place them in the correct holes, other than that, this is the only critical area.

5) Unfortunately, the screw holes do not have any countersink (space withing the drilled hole to hide the screw head) so that the heads of the screws do not stick out slightly from the surface. HOWEVER: If you're familiar with woodworking you can drill the countersink holes yourself but be very careful of the depth because the material is not all that think and you don't want to drill all the way through. Otherwise, if you don't drill your own countersink holes, just be sure your properly screw the supplied screws in as far as they will go BUT DO NOT OVER TIGHTEN THEM BECAUSE THE MATERIAL IS TOO POROUS FOR THAT AND THEY WILL NEVER BE AS TIGHT AS THEY WOULD BE IF THE MATERIAL WAS REAL WOOD - THIS IS WHY YOU MUST USE GLUE WHEN ASSEMBLING THIS BOOKCASE.

Overall, my build turned out OK, but only because I used wood glue on all joints. I would have given this review 5 stars but because of the lack of countersunk screw holes and the need for glue to ensure sturdiness it gets a 3 star.

I would recommend this ONLY if you're familiar with assembling wood products and know how to use wood glue to ensure tight joints. This is not a difficult project and for the price this is not a bad bookcase if you know how to use wood glue.

I would NOT recommend this if you've never built knock-down furniture and/or you're expecting a really solid bookcase when completed.

This is a review after 3 months of usage, spoiler alert, I’m pretty happy with it.*


I bought this 27inch 1440p 180Hz (KG271U N3bmiipx) monitor for around 170 usd with offer and taxes.


Pros:

1. 2K, very fast 180hz refresh rate, with built in speakers for 170 USD.

2. Pretty high color range (DCI-P3 95%), not verified, but to naked eye, love the vivid colour accurate display, this was important to me.

3. IPS screen, meaning good viewing angles, also important for good viewing experience.

4. Decent HDR for an IPS LCD budget monitor.

5. Didn't notice any flickering.


Reasons for asterisk:

1. In standard or other modes, even when set to 100, brightness feels low in well lit environments. Turning HDR mode on solves this issue, probably because of increased peak brightness, but this makes it too bright in dark environments, you won't be able to adjust screen brightness in HDR mode. 2. Overshooting is noticeable to naked eye if overdrive setting is set as extreme. Recommend setting it to minimum, or off, then it’s not at all noticeable.

3. Speakers are like what you’d expect in your typical gaming monitors. Pretty mediocre, will get the job done. They lack any base or instrument clarity or separation. In movies or songs, vocals are pretty crisp, but the background music sounds pretty low. Could be solved with headphones or speakers.

4. HDMI connections only supports upto 144hz.

5. Lack of height adjustment for stand.

6. Felt like a thick monitor, build quality is decent, all plastic, does not give you premium feels, but good for it's price.


At this point you might be thinking, why did this guy give 5 stars when the cons list is bigger than pros. It's because I compared this with similarly priced Sansui ESA-G27F6Q and Arzopa M1RC side by side, and overall Acer seemed like the best pick in this price range.

text:
DOWNGRADED to one star on September 24, 2024: In addition to the issues with the firmware and software described below, the drive started getting very hot, crashing the computer, and failing to be detected at boot time until I shut the computer down and waited for it to cool off. When I secure-erased my data before sending it back to Samsung, I found many unwritable blocks and bad sector errors. Sent it back to Samsung and all they did was re-flash the already up-to-date firmware and erase the drive. Believe the one-star reviews.

=====================================================

The physical hardware is [NOT] fine. It does [NOT] what it says on the tin. However, there were both firmware and software issues that make it a three-star and not a five-star product. They cost me a lot of time.

First, there is a known firmware bug that causes it to wear out more quickly, and although I bought my drive a year after that bug was fixed, and the box said the drive was manufactured nine months after the fix, I still got a drive with the old firmware, which I discovered only after fully loading it from my old SSD. They are apparently, as of March 2024, still shipping the old drives in new boxes.

Second, I made the mistake of cloning the drive with Samsung Magician. This software's data migration is garbage. Although it faithfully copied the disk, it put the WinRE partition at the front of the drive and deactivated it. After several hours, I figured out how to re-create it at the end of the drive and activate it, but there is still wasted space at the beginning of the drive. Searching the Internet, I found another user who had the same issue with this software in 2019. In five years, they don't bother to fix this design flaw? Apparently not.

Long ago, I worked in computer technology, and my boss referred to the industry trend as "code and throw." Code it and throw it out to the users with minimal testing. Apparently, this is Samsung's policy, at least with this firmware and software.
label: feature_evaluation

I had no issue with my previous Samsung 980. I bought a Samsung 990 PRO SSD 4 TB on November 18, 2024 from Amazon. I had no trouble transferring my data from my previous NVME. It worked flawlessly in my PC for about 6 months. Then suddenly it would spontaneously reboot my computer and then fail to be detected so my system would just be sitting on the BIOS screen. It would take a hard shut off and turn on to get it to work again. So I foolishly bought another Samsung 990 PRO SSD 4 TB on July 20, 2025 from Amazon. I had no trouble transferring my data from the previous Samsung 990 PRO SSD 4 TB. The problem then disappeared completely with the new 990 PRO.

Now, two months later with again no changes to my system in any way... the problem is back on the new 990 PRO. I wish I would have read reviews of other people having this exact same problem. The Magician app shows it is failing randomly when the NVME is as cool as 38 degrees centigrade.

I have been in professional IT for 30 years and have never experienced something like this. Either these have a design issue that many other people are experiencing based on reviews or I have been incredibly unlucky.

I have used Samsung SSD drives for many years exclusively. They have always been the fastest, most reliable SSD drives you could buy. They were more expensive...but worth it.

This one...definitely not. It's very fast. However it has a critical design issue that I wish I had known about before I bought it, which makes it very unreliable.

I purchased this drive for a new PC build. It worked great for three months. After that, at random times, the drive began to vanish. It would disappear as if it had been unplugged. If the PC was using it as its system drive (and it was), the PC would crash and reboot to a BIOS screen. Rebooting the PC does not fix it, the PC has to be physically power cycled for the drive to come back up and reappear.

No data was lost...but it became extremely unreliable, crashing and disappearing more than once a day. I opened a warranty ticket with Samsung, and they replaced it, no questions asked.

Two months later...the replacement drive they provided is now doing the exact same thing. I now have ANOTHER warranty replacement claim open with Samsung.

I did a search online, and there are MANY people complaining about this problem with the Samsung 990 drive. There is obviously something very wrong with the design of the drive, but this problem is known and widespread.

For this reason I recommend you do NOT buy this drive.

Buy it for its versatility for top-up and emergency use. It's not best-in-class for charging performance, but it's quite convenient for gap-filling. 5 stars for convenience, 4 stars for wired charging performance, and 2-3 stars for wireless. Judge according to your priorities.

This is the on-the-road charging swiss army knife. It has both USB-C and lightning cables built-in (never again "where did I put that cable?") It has a clear digital charge readout that mostly seems accurate. It's bit heavier than other 10Ah-class batteries, but it's smaller (and thicker) so it'll fit into most pockets and pretty much all bags.

Some performance numbers follow. Note that I tested with high-end Apple devices. If yours is older (and thus consumes less), your performance will be better, so treat this as the worst-case scenario.

Wired charging is fine. A 15-minute charge of an iPhone 17 Pro filled it by about 20%, at about a 1:1 charge rating (the Ridge lost 20% of charge). This suggests that you get a bit more than one full phone charge out of this battery. The same 15 minutes on an iPad Pro (M4) get you 10% at a 1:2 rating. You'll be able to fill about 50-60% of that iPad with a full Ridge battery. (The iPad Pro battery is larger than the Ridge's.)

Wireless charging is nothing of the sort. Think of it as keeping your device's battery from draining while you're "charging" but not much more. This isn't wireless inefficiency; there just isn't very much juice flowing. You can slap the Ridge at the back of your iPhone and preserve its battery until the Ridge runs out, but your phone battery won't get any fuller on the way. This is also true for Watch "charging" - an Apple Watch Ultra 2 gained +2% in 15 minutes. Kinda useless in practice.

Note that this isn't a problem with wireless charging. If you (bring and) plug an Apple wireless charging disk into the Ridge's USB-C port, your phone or watch will charge. This is a limitation of the onboard wireless hardware or software on the Ridge.

MagSafe charging is... fine... if your goal is simply attaching a battery to the back of your phone. My phone loses charge faster than this thing can put it back.

And then there's the heat.

This thing gets HOT. Not "slightly warm." More like "did I accidentally buy a tiny hand warmer?" Forget tossing it in your pocket while charging unless you're trying to roast your leg.

What's most disappointing is that I own a generic, no-name 20W power bank that cost less, charges itself much faster, charges two phones over the course of a day, and doesn't feel like it's preparing for atmospheric re-entry.

I really wanted this to be my everyday battery pack because it looks fantastic.

Instead, it's become the nicest-looking battery pack sitting unused in my desk drawer.

Two stars because the design deserves the credit. Unfortunately, the performance doesn't.
